Lessons.Title: Powers of 10 PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L02 recognizes repeated factors of ten and exponential notation through billion; the OPTIONAL extension considers one trillion. A power10^k has k factors of10, so source place-value scale must be verified, not merely counting printed digits.

Warm-up How Many Do You See Starburst uses publisher diagram with successively subdivided line segments; source visual number of extensions cannot be certified from plain text without the actual image. Teacher assesses the learner's own grouped count and drawing.

Activity1 Population of Delaware and India: original source says ABOUT1,000,000 in Delaware and ABOUT1,000,000,000 in India in1997. These are historical educational benchmarks, not asserted current population facts. One million=10^6=1000 thousands; one billion=10^9=1000 millions and1000000 thousands. Original source asks how many times to extend pictured segments, requiring teacher visual review.

Activity2 source exact equations 2000=?×20 =>100;20×10×?=20000 =>100;?×10=100000 =>10000;1000×10000=10000000. Printed exponent questions10^3=1000,10^4=10000,10^7=10000000. Learner explains factors of10 and why exponents count them.

Optional Activity3 source one trillion=1000000000000=10^12, equal1000 billions or1000000 millions; source asks an OPEN real-world example with appropriate estimation and caveat. No student-generated claims about actual physical counts should be pregraded. Original gated Cool-down separately unavailable; Edulytiks independent teacher Cool-down tests a new power.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: represent very large whole numbers with powers of ten and explain how many groups of one thousand, one million or one billion compose them. The 2021 source uses HISTORICAL human-population examples, including India in 1997, so those figures must not be described as a current census. The optional trillion exploration is modeling rather than an official factual count.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: extend a first-party text pattern: a unit strip divided into ten equal segments, then each segment into ten, and repeat to obtain ten, one hundred and one thousand tiny segments. Explain how 10×10×10=1000 and the notation 10^3 refer to three factors of ten.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — name and relate scales: 1,000,000=10^6 is one thousand groups of one thousand or one million; 1,000,000,000=10^9 is one thousand groups of one million and one million groups of one thousand. Write both in words and expanded products of powers of ten. Discuss why a familiar local population might help students visualize scale without asserting an unverified current population.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — missing factors: solve 3000=30×100, 24×10×100=24000, and (missing number)×10=100000 (missing10000). Read 10^3,10^4,10^7 as 1000,10000,10000000. Optional: name 10^12 as one trillion and explain why claiming a real-world exact trillion-count would require separate trustworthy evidence.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: mathematical notation and numeric blanks can be checked, but explaining diagrams, describing orders of magnitude and proposing a plausible real-world example demand teacher review. Original publisher images and restricted answers not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exponent counts tens
KeyConcepts.Definition: The exponent on a positive integer power of ten counts how many ten factors are multiplied.
KeyConcepts.Example: Six factors of ten form a million.

KeyConcepts.Title: Large unit groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: A billion can be expressed as a thousand millions or a million thousands.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing ten-power factors
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplication identities help determine unknown powers without arbitrary zero insertion.

Lessons.Title: Metric Conversion and Multiplication by Powers of Ten
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: convert from a LARGER metric length unit to a smaller unit by multiplying by 100 or1000, and use the context of athletics to compare jump lengths while selecting appropriate units. The source asks students to notice relationships across conversion tables and defend units in a broad jump story.

Warm-up: point to a meter stick and explain that it has 100 centimeters and 1000 millimeters. State that 1 kilometer has1000 meters and that a centimeter has ten millimeters. Predict why a large unit needs MORE smaller-sized units for the same physical distance.

Activity 1 — equivalent length tables: convert 3.2 meters to320 centimeters and3200 millimeters; convert12 kilometers to12000 meters. Use a first-party accessible length table and distinguish metric linear units, not square or cubic ones. Explain how multiplying by100 or1000 changes the VALUE of each digit in the new unit rather than physically changing distance.

Activity 2 — first-party standing jumps: students measure 1.62 meters,1.39 meters and1.50 meters; a hypothetical class comparison benchmark is1.45 meters (145 cm). Classify the first and third as above and the second below the benchmark. Convert each jump into centimeters and millimeters; discuss why reporting 1620 millimeters sounds numerically larger than162 centimeters while describing the identical distance.

Teacher boundary: the source asks students to classify physical measurements, analyze a published jump record, debate units and explain equivalence; a conversion calculator may verify values but cannot certify measurement interpretation or choice of helpful units. No source athlete photo reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Meter to centimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: One meter contains100 centimeters, so meter quantities multiply by100 when expressed in centimeters.

KeyConcepts.Title: Meter to millimeter and kilometer to meter
KeyConcepts.Definition: One meter contains1000 millimeters and one kilometer contains1000 meters.
KeyConcepts.Example: Do not confuse the two different starting units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare in common units
KeyConcepts.Definition: To compare a jump and a benchmark, first convert their measurements to compatible units.
KeyConcepts.Example: The same physical jump has equivalent numerical descriptions.

WorkedExamples.Method: Independently authored place-value/measurement representation with exact unit check and teacher-reviewed explanation.
Steps: Label each result in the target unit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert a long race
WorkedExamples.Question: Express12km in meters.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independently authored place-value/measurement representation with exact unit check and teacher-reviewed explanation.
Steps: Identify the number as a distance, not an area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare hypothetical broad jumps
WorkedExamples.Question: Three jump lengths are1.62m,1.39m and1.50m. Which are above1.45m?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independently authored place-value/measurement representation with exact unit check and teacher-reviewed explanation.
Steps: Explain why 1.62 and1.50 are longer than the benchmark.
WorkedExamples.Answer: First and third are above; second is below.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Divide by100 when converting meters to centimeters
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A smaller unit produces a larger number of units for the same length.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Compare digits without matching measurement units
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert both to centimeters or both to meters before ordering.

SummaryPoints: Larger metric lengths convert to smaller metric units with positive factors of ten.
Unit conversion changes a count, not the actual distance.
Measuring jumps and explaining an appropriate unit are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Metric Conversion and Division by Powers of Ten
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: express measurements from a SMALLER metric unit in a larger unit and explain the meaning of dividing by100 or1000 in a place-value chart. The source's athlete event table and running-distance table require interpretation of what each shifted digit represents and a peer-reviewed argument of why the method works.

Warm-up: contrast 750 centimeters with750 meters. Dividing 750cm by100 gives7.5 meters, but dividing 750 meters by100 would answer a different question. Keep the source unit attached throughout conversion.

Activity 1 — convert event measurements: a fictional long jump is745cm=7.45m, a throwing event has length4567cm=45.67m, and a shot put is1580cm=15.8m. Estimate each physical magnitude and explain why centimeter precision may be used for athletic measurement even when meters are more intuitive for description.

Activity 2 — road distances: 9513 meters=9.513 kilometers, 11018 meters=11.018 kilometers, and10000m=10km. Explain that dividing the count by1000 changes the number of units because each new kilometer is one thousand meters. A student who says the decimal point merely 'moves' without interpreting meters and kilometers must explain the place-value units.

Assessment: an exact numeric conversion is machine-checkable, but identifying original and target unit, interpreting athletic distances and critiquing the validity of a general place-shift strategy require teacher review. Original source athlete photographs and protected responses not copied.

KeyConcepts.Definition: Convert a centimeter count to meters by dividing by100.

KeyConcepts.Title: Meter to kilometer
KeyConcepts.Definition: Convert from meters to kilometers by dividing by1000.

KeyConcepts.Title: Explain decimal place value
KeyConcepts.Definition: Changing the measurement unit changes the count associated with the same length.
KeyConcepts.Example: Every tenfold shift can be explained through new place-value unit size.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use the centimeter-to-meter factor for a meter-to-kilometer conversion
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The two target units have different scale relationships.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 100 for centimeters per meter and1000 for meters per kilometer.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Describe a digit 'shifting' without naming the changed unit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Place-value reasoning should explain the number of smaller units inside a larger one.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label both endpoints and why one target unit contains100 or1000 of the source units.

SummaryPoints: Convert cm→m by dividing100 and m→km by dividing1000.
Verify conversions with inverse multiplication.
Student explanation of place-value changes and useful unit selection remains teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Multi-step Conversion Problems: Metric Length
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve MULTI-STEP length situations involving centimeter steps, meter totals and kilometer distances, then compare weekly runners after making their units compatible. The source asks learners to choose appropriate units and compare several strategies for sum and difference, not just copy conversion ratios.

Warm-up: a typical step may be measured in centimeters; a day-long walk is easier to express in meters or kilometers. Discuss the meaning of a 0.52-meter step and why 8000 repeated steps produce a distance above4km, conditional on constant stride length.

Activity 1 — count steps: assume a measured half-meter-ish stride of52cm and8000 steps in a day. Multiply52×8000=416000 centimeters, then divide100 to4160 meters or divide100000 to4.16km. Check equivalence by converting0.52m×8000 directly to4160m. State this is an idealized constant-step model, not a measured personal activity record.

Activity 2 — two weekly runners: one runner's fictional kilometer totals are 5.5,6.25,4.75,7.1,6.4 for five days, summing exactly30.0km. Another's meter totals are5400,6200,5800,6500,7000m, summing30900m=30.9km. The second runner traveled0.9km farther. Explain why direct comparison of30 and30900 without units is invalid.

Assessment: actual individual stride measurement or partner work, choice of unit, estimated realism, adding daily distances, conversion reasoning and a written comparison are teacher-reviewed. Numeric totals can support the result but cannot certify the real-life modeling assumptions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated step length
KeyConcepts.Definition: Approximate constant stride length multiplied by step count estimates total distance.
KeyConcepts.Example: This assumes a consistent average step length.

KeyConcepts.Title: Centimeters, meters and kilometers
KeyConcepts.Example: All three describe the same physical length.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sum and compare in one unit
KeyConcepts.Definition: A pair of weekly travel totals may be compared only when in compatible units.
KeyConcepts.Example: The numerical digits alone are insufficient.

WorkedExamples.Question: Find total km for5.5,6.25,4.75,7.1,6.4km.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independently authored place-value/measurement representation with exact unit check and teacher-reviewed explanation.
WorkedExamples.Check: All values have the same km unit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare a second week
WorkedExamples.Question: The other distances are5400,6200,5800,6500,7000 meters. Who went farther?
WorkedExamples.Method: Independently authored place-value/measurement representation with exact unit check and teacher-reviewed explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Compare unconverted kilometer and meter totals as printed numbers
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert both to km or both to m before comparing.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat an assumed constant step length as a guaranteed measured distance
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The model assumes each step has approximately the same length.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label result an estimate; discuss measurement variability.

SummaryPoints: Multi-step conversions preserve the physical quantity across cm, m and km.
Choose convenient units and check comparisons only after alignment.
Teacher reviews estimation assumptions and student method explanations.

Lessons.Title: Multi-step Conversion Problems: Metric Liquid Volume
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: convert LITERS to MILLILITERS and back, including decimals and fractions, then solve a multi-step liquid-volume problem involving dancers sharing bottled water. The original source asks students to compare whether they convert each bottle first or convert total liters last, and to explain which strategy is helpful.

Warm-up: contrast a bottle of capacity0.45L with a 20L cooler. One liter is1000 milliliters, so0.45L=450mL and20L=20000mL. Explain why a container image alone cannot determine capacity without labeled measurements; publisher bottle artwork not reused.

Activity 1 — unit table and comparisons: convert5L to5000mL; 0.95L to950mL;6500mL to6.5L; and3/4L to750mL. Compare15mL with0.15L and explain 0.15L=150mL, so15mL is smaller. Explain how a missing zero in 0.015L changes the interpretation.

Activity 2 — original dancers problem: 24 dancers each drink one and a half 450mL bottles during a rehearsal. Total volume24×1.5×450=16200mL, or16.2L. If the water began in a 20L cooler, 3.8L remains under the ideal no-spill assumption. A student may compute0.45L×1.5×24 or calculate total bottles first; compare strategies and state that bottles consumed may include halves.

Assessment: unit table numerical conversions are partial automatable checks, but the source multi-step modeling, physically meaningful capacity and comparison of converting before/after multiplication require teacher review. Gated source responses and original source image assets remain unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Liters and milliliters
KeyConcepts.Definition: One liter of liquid volume equals one thousand milliliters.
KeyConcepts.Example: Multiply L by1000; divide mL by1000.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fractions of a liter
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction such as3/4L is equivalent to a decimal fraction times1000 milliliters.
KeyConcepts.Example: The unit and denominator must refer to the same liter.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent multi-step strategies
KeyConcepts.Definition: Convert the bottle first or compute total mL first; multiplication and unit conversion should reconcile.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiply by100 instead of1000 when converting liters to milliliters
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Milli indicates thousandths of one liter.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add 24 dancers and1.5 bottles as though quantities were comparable

CommonMistakes.Correction: Compute dancers×bottles per dancer×mL per bottle.

SummaryPoints: One liter contains1000 milliliters and fractional liters convert consistently.
Multi-step volume problems can be solved in either liter or milliliter units.
